question: For a finite Gaussian teacher–student two-layer ReLU population loss, which symmetric spurious-minimum families become saddles as one or two student neurons are added, and through which Hessian subspaces does the transition occur?

key_findings.claim: The analysis isolates a highly structured population-risk model with exact row/column permutation symmetries.
key_findings.evidence: Inputs are standard Gaussian, the target hidden-weight matrix is the identity up to orthogonal transformation, teacher and student second-layer weights are fixed to positive ones via ReLU homogeneity, the student has k at least d neurons, and the expected squared loss is studied at fixed critical points rather than along training trajectories.

key_findings.claim: Fractional-power-series parameterizations turn families indexed by input dimension into fixed-dimensional analytic objects.
key_findings.evidence: Critical points with isotropy Delta(S_{d-p} x S_p) lie in fixed-point spaces whose dimension is independent of d for fixed excess width. Regular families admit convergent Puiseux/fractional power series in d, enabling asymptotic loss and Hessian calculations.

anchors.section: A.1 Fractional power series for type-II minima

key_findings.claim: For the maximally symmetric type-I family, one extra neuron creates exactly d-1 descent directions in the standard-representation sector.
key_findings.evidence: The Delta S_d family is a spurious minimum at k=d and a nondegenerate saddle at k=d+1. The new negative Hessian eigenvalue has multiplicity d-1, while the other displayed standard-representation eigenvalues and the high-multiplicity sectors remain positive asymptotically.

anchors.section: 5.1 Critical points of isotropy Delta S_d

key_findings.claim: Less symmetric Delta(S_{d-1} x S_1) type-I and type-II minima survive one added neuron and require two to become saddles.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4 states that these regular families are spurious minima for k=d and d+1 and nondegenerate saddles for k=d+2, with at least d-2 descent directions. For the relevant 2d by 2d Hessian principal block, the leading eigenvalues are approximately 0.8060 and -0.1198; Cauchy interlacing transfers negative curvature to the full Hessian.

key_findings.claim: Most Hessian directions remain positively curved and highly skewed; annihilation is localized to symmetry-selected low-dimensional sectors.
key_findings.evidence: For fixed k-d and p in {0,1}, Theorem 3 places kd-Theta(d) eigenvalues in two representation sectors at 1/4 minus or plus 1/(2 pi), up to O(d^-1/4), both positive. Negative eigenvalues arise in standard rather than exterior-square or partition-(d-2,2) sectors.

key_findings.claim: Adding neurons changes stability while leaving leading loss values almost unchanged for the analyzed branches.
key_findings.evidence: For type-II Delta(S_{d-1} x S_1) families, loss remains Theta(1/d), with the leading coefficient moving from about 2.9736 at k=d to about 2.6725 and 2.6719 at k=d+1,d+2. Type-I leading loss remains 1/2-1/pi across the displayed excess widths.

key_findings.claim: The spectral transition persists under sufficiently small asymmetric perturbations of the target, but only locally around nondegenerate analyzed critical points.
key_findings.evidence: Because the minimum-to-saddle transition occurs away from integer-dimensional degeneracy, the implicit-function/continuity argument gives a neighborhood of the orthogonal target where nearby critical points retain the same number of negative eigenvalues. This does not classify arbitrary asymmetric targets or all critical points.

anchors.section: Concluding comments on forced symmetry breaking

key_findings.claim: Overparameterization also fossilizes critical points into degenerate simplicial complexes, so annihilation of selected nondegenerate families is not a globally benign-landscape theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A.7 shows that adding neurons replaces global minima and more general critical points by connected simplicial sets with zero Hessian directions where differentiable, while new nondegenerate points can appear. The main analysis deliberately follows particular regular branches.

anchors.section: A.7 Adding more than two neurons
Fossilization of critical points, general case

method.core_idea: Exploit exact permutation symmetries to classify selected critical-point branches by isotropy, express them as Puiseux series in dimension, decompose the Hessian into irreducible representation sectors, and detect width-induced negative curvature through spectral asymptotics and interlacing.
method.mechanism: Restrict the equivariant gradient to a low-dimensional fixed-point space; continue regular critical points across d; solve fractional-power-series coefficient equations, partly by Newton–Raphson; translate isotropy into isotypic Hessian blocks; express high-multiplicity eigenvalues through vanishing gradient coefficients; calculate standard/trivial blocks; use a principal block and Cauchy interlacing to prove full-Hessian descent directions when neurons are added.
assumptions: Inputs follow the d-dimensional standard Gaussian distribution
Labels come from a realizable two-layer ReLU teacher with orthogonal hidden weights
Second-layer teacher and student weights are fixed positive and normalized to ones
The objective is population squared loss without biases or finite-sample noise
Excess width k-d is fixed while d is sufficiently large
Critical-point families are regular, analytic, and nondegenerate where required
The principal isotropy types are Delta S_d or Delta(S_{d-1} x S_1)
Fractional-series remainders do not change the reported signs at the dimensions in scope

techniques.role: Organizes spurious minima by isotropy subgroups of row/column permutations.
Turns a growing d-by-k problem into a constant-dimensional analytic vector field.
Computes dimension-dependent critical points, losses, and spectra asymptotically.
Reduces a huge Hessian to small blocks indexed by irreducible representations.
Evaluates high-multiplicity eigenvalues through coefficients that vanish at criticality.
Certifies negative curvature in the full Hessian from a two-row principal block.
Describes degenerate simplicial critical sets created by neuron splitting.

limitations: The model is a two-layer, bias-free, fixed-output-weight Gaussian teacher–student population objective.
Only selected regular symmetry families are classified; lower-symmetry or newly created critical points can remain.
Many signs are asymptotic for sufficiently large d with O(d^-1/4) or related remainder terms.
Some Puiseux coefficients are obtained numerically with Newton–Raphson rather than closed-form certified arithmetic.
Turning a minimum into a saddle does not prove SGD reaches or follows the resulting descent directions from random initialization.
The local perturbation result does not extend to arbitrary asymmetric teachers or non-Gaussian data.
Finite empirical-risk noise, trainable second-layer weights, biases, depth, and common regularizers are absent.
The appendix proves neuron splitting also creates degenerate critical complexes and potentially new branches.
No end-to-end experimental evaluation tests the quantitative spectrum predictions.
failure_modes: An unstudied lower-symmetry spurious minimum survives the claimed mild overparameterization.
Finite d remainders reverse an eigenvalue whose leading asymptotic term is small.
Newton–Raphson converges to one fractional-series branch while missing another regular family.
A saddle's negative eigenspace has a tiny basin-aligned projection, so practical SGD still stalls.
Trainable output weights introduce scaling degeneracy and additional critical geometry.
Non-Gaussian or finite-sample inputs destroy the exact group invariance and low-dimensional fixed spaces.
Neuron splitting produces flat critical manifolds where Hessian sign alone is insufficient.
A perturbation outside the implicit-function neighborhood changes the critical-point count or Morse index.
reusable_insights: Use data/model symmetries to block-diagonalize a loss Hessian before attempting brute-force spectral analysis.
Track critical-point branches as capacity changes instead of comparing unrelated optima across widths.
A few added parameters can change curvature in a small representation sector while leaving loss almost unchanged.
Principal-submatrix interlacing can certify escape directions without computing a full Hessian.
Report which families are annihilated and which new or degenerate critical sets appear; avoid global benign-landscape language.
Stress-test asymptotic sign claims with finite-d interval bounds and random perturbations.
open_questions: Do all practically reachable spurious minima fall into the analyzed high-symmetry families?
What is the smallest excess width that removes every non-global attractor at fixed d?
Can finite-d computer-assisted bounds certify the Puiseux sign predictions without asymptotic ambiguity?
How do trainable output weights, biases, regularization, or depth alter the standard-representation mechanism?
Can stochastic optimization be proved to align with the newly created descent subspaces?
Which parts persist for empirical risk and non-Gaussian structured data?
Can fossilized flat complexes themselves attract or delay SGD despite lacking strict local minima?

competitive_landscape.title: Spurious Local Minima are Common in Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct foundational analysis of the same Gaussian teacher–student population loss
competitive_landscape.difference: Safran and Shamir give computer-assisted existence results and SGD evidence for spurious minima at matched width and observe that overparameterization helps; this paper classifies symmetry branches and analytically locates the Hessian directions and neuron counts that change their stability.

competitive_landscape.title: The Effects of Mild Over-parameterization on the Optimization Landscape of Shallow ReLU Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Safran, Yehudai, and Shamir show under technical conditions that adding one neuron turns a given non-global minimum into a saddle and analyze most-direction convexity; this paper shows specific lower-symmetry branches can remain minima at k=d+1 and require k=d+2, with exact representation-theoretic descent multiplicities.

competitive_landscape.title: Student Specialization in Deep Rectified Networks With Finite Width and Input Dimension
competitive_landscape.difference: Tian proves neuron specialization under small per-example gradients and augmented finite datasets, extending to deep ReLU/Leaky-ReLU networks; this paper analyzes population-loss critical curvature under Gaussian symmetry and does not provide an SGD sample-complexity guarantee.

competitive_landscape.title: A Mean Field View of the Landscape of Two-Layers Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Mei, Montanari, and Nguyen pass to a mean-field PDE and prove convergence in selected scaling-limit examples; this paper stays at finite excess width and resolves local Hessian mechanisms that limiting descriptions can average away.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Representation theory, algebraic geometry, Puiseux series, and interlacing reveal a finite mechanism by which one or two added ReLU neurons annihilate symmetric spurious minima while leaving loss nearly unchanged.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper constructs regular critical branches, derives high-multiplicity spectral asymptotics, proves exact descent-space dimensions for two isotropy types, extends Morse indices to small target perturbations, and describes degenerate critical complexes created by neuron splitting.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The genuinely new insight is that mild overparameterization is symmetry-selective: one neuron suffices for maximal symmetry but not for a prominent lower-symmetry family. The result is mathematically detailed yet narrow; it is not evidence that general deep-network landscapes become benign or that SGD exploits these directions.

Claims are restricted to the stated regular branches and sufficiently large dimensions; no global all-minima or practical-SGD conclusion is inferred.
